transcript.text: As great as the heart is, it wouldn't be much good to us without some great vessels connecting it to the rest of the circulatory system, so let's take a look at these great vessels that attach to the heart. We'll start with the superior vena cava, which drains deoxygenated blood from the upper half of the body. We see we have a right internal jugular vein draining the head and neck, and we have a right subclavian vein draining the right upper limb, and together they'll form the right brachiosephalic vein. Brachiosephalic refers to upper limb and head, and finally that will enter into the SVC. It's variable, but usually the right inferior thyroid veins are also going to drain into the brachiosephalic right before it goes into the SVC. Similarly, on the left side we have a left internal jugular vein, we have a left subclavian vein, and they'll form the left brachiosephalic vein, which is quite a bit longer than the right because it has to cross over the midline to reach the SVC over on the right side of the heart. It also tends to receive the inferior thyroid veins on that side before joining the SVC, and although it wasn't pictured on the right side, the brachiosephalics also tend to receive the internal thoracic or mammary veins. If we remove the veins, we can see our aortic arch a lot better. So here we have our aortic arch, and this first very large branch we see is something called the brachiosephalic trunk. And as the name implies, it's going to supply the upper limb and head and neck. And so it will branch into a right common carotid artery supplying the head and neck, and a right subclavian artery supplying the upper limb. And here's where we have a bit of a symmetry, because the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries arise directly from the arch. Therefore, there is no left brachiosephalic trunk. There's just the one. And the subclavian has some notable branches that are descriptive in their names, including fyroservical, costoservical, and vertebral. They basically tell you what they're going to supply. And we've already seen that the internal thoracic or mammary arteries arise from the subclavian. Now let's take a look from the left side, where we can see our ascending aorta becoming an arch, the aortic arch, and then finally posteriorly becoming the descending aorta as it heads towards the abdomen. And it's going to go through that hiatus, the aortic hiatus, in the diaphragm in order to reach the abdominal cavity. We'll go back to an anterior view, and we're going to remove the aorta to see the pulmonary trunk and its branches better. We see the pulmonary trunk is pretty short before it branches into the right and left main pulmonary arteries. And if we swing around to the left, we can see it again with, again, a very short trunk forming almost a T-shaped intersection where it bifurcates into the left and right pulmonary arteries. Here we see the left pulmonary artery coming right at us and towards the hyalum of the lung. We also see a tiny bit of connective tissue between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta called the ligamentum arteriosum, which if we recall from fetal circulation is the leftover remnants of that fetal bypass called the ductus arteriosus. And it's connecting, again, to the aortic arch, which in this case we see that it's going over the right pulmonary artery before moving leftward to cross over the left main bronchus. And this is what we mean when we say an arch is a left-sided arch or a leftward arch. When you learn about congenital heart diseases, you'll hear that term, and a left-sided arch is the more common arrangement. But you might hear the term right-sided arch, and in that case, it will cross over the right main bronchus.
